inserts.title: Recordings isolate target echoes
paragraphs: Simmons recorded the outgoing call and the returning echo from a target at 30 cm. The echo arrived after the call, not at the same moment as the sound leaving the bat. Sound from the apparatus also appeared in the recording. The investigator separated target echoes from that other returning sound before measuring the delay.

In the experimental conditions, the echo from that target returned about 1.7 ms after the call. Electronic delay channels could change this interval directly. The loudspeakers kept fixed physical positions while the timing changed. Direct control over echo timing gave the experimenter a clean test of the ranging cue, with no physical movement required. Simulated range changed without moving anything.

Simmons recorded outgoing sounds and echoes while bats discriminated target distance. Each echo in the recording can be matched to the call that produced it. The recordings thus show the timing that bats had available during the task. Each recording pairs one outgoing sound with the echo that follows it. That pairing makes the delay readable directly.
notes: Recordings isolate target echoes.

Simmons recorded the outgoing call and the returning echo from a target at 30 cm

inserts.title: Choices and prediction are separate curves
paragraphs: The measured curve shows the bats' actual choices at each difference between two targets. The other curve is a prediction that Simmons published from the recorded signal. The other curve comes from calculation, not from behavior. Each point on the measured curve counts correct choices at one difference. Both curves appear on one set of axes.

A matched receiver is a proposed interpretation of that agreement. It is not a demonstrated neural mechanism. Its role is to predict the curves, not to name neurons. Neurons that perform the matching were not identified in this study. Simmons described the receiver as a functional hypothesis. Its prediction was derived from the signal, not fitted to the choices.

Simmons plotted both curves at 30 cm, the same distance used for the measured choices. The prediction used a signal that the bats had produced. The result sets a behavioral measure beside a signal-based prediction, not a single cell's response. Both curves cover differences from millimeters to several centimeters. The match holds across that whole range.

inserts.title: Jitter rises as the broadcast weakens
paragraphs: The cochlear-nucleus broadcast peak had mean jitter values of 32, 44 and 67 μs at −30, −40 and −50 dB attenuation. The three settings differ in how loud the stimulus was. Greater attenuation makes the stimulus weaker. Timing was least precise at the quietest setting. The jitter values were reported for the same cochlear-nucleus peak.

A response can arrive several milliseconds after a sound and still repeat within tens of microseconds. Mean delay and repeatability are separate measures of the same response. Latency and jitter answer different questions about one event. The broadcast peak was late, but its repeats were tight. Each value in these recordings was a repeatability measure, not a delay.

Across the delays, the jitter changed only slightly. That stability held within each sound level. Sound level, not echo delay, set the size of the jitter. The seven delays covered the full cascade used in the study. Those seven delays were tested at all three sound levels. The first-echo jitter values are reported in the same figure.

Those cochlear-nucleus latencies were measured in the same animals.

The consistency of the waveform across repetitions is a separate property. Extra processing time by itself says little about precision. This property was measured separately from the latency. Early midbrain peaks stayed closely aligned from one repetition to the next. Those responses were recorded from the same stimuli at both sites. Each peak was measured for its own timing.

The midbrain data came from the same animals as the cochlear-nucleus data. Identical stimuli and timing measures were applied at both sites. This design isolates the midbrain step from differences in animals or stimuli. Each site produced its own latency and its own jitter values. Those jitter values were close to the cochlear-nucleus values. Both sites showed that pattern.

inserts.title: The decoder remains untested
paragraphs: The recordings were digitized at 20 kHz. That rate places important constraints on very small timing estimates. Sampling at that rate sets how precisely a latency can be measured. Restricted recording sites add a second limit on interpretation. The recordings were made under anesthesia, so they describe no ongoing behavior. The timing values come from averages across trials.

The behavioral and neural values come from different tasks and preparations. The brainstem data explain only part of one-microsecond perception, because its variability stayed larger. The behavioral value comes from specialized tasks. The neural value comes from anesthetized recordings. Each number answers a different question about timing. The neural values measure population timing, not perception.

The authors identified precisely timed population signals as candidate inputs to a range readout. The experiment never directly identified such a decoder. Precisely timed population signals are one proposed input to that computation. The authors offered that idea without testing a decoder. The recordings supply the timing data for such a model. The proposal is about population timing, not single neurons.
notes: The decoder remains untested.

inserts.title: Two-tone timing reveals inhibitory arrival
paragraphs: The two-tone experiment reveals suppression that recordings of isolated tones alone would miss. A sideband can suppress a response without producing a visible response when presented by itself. That is why the paired-tone test is needed. The inhibitory tone outlasted the excitatory one in these pairs. Both tones were presented to the same neuron. Those tones defined the test.

The method infers when inhibition becomes effective at the recorded neuron. Experiments that vary acoustic timing reveal the functional timing of inhibition. The measured quantity is functional timing, not a direct recording of synaptic current. Each tone interval in the series gave one data point. The timing is an estimate from the tone sequence. The measurement is indirect.

The 5-ms excitatory tone was shorter than the 20-ms inhibitory tone. Its onset could fall before, during or after the excitatory tone as the interval varied. Each interval produced its own level of suppression. The response was measured as the drop in excitatory firing. The same neuron was used across all intervals. Each pair was one test.
notes: Two-tone timing reveals inhibitory arrival.

inserts.title: Two blockers, one neuron
paragraphs: The three conditions were obtained from the same neuron. Differences between the two blockers could not be explained by sampling different neurons. Baseline, gabazine and strychnine conditions were all measured in that one cell. The design kept neuron identity constant across conditions, which makes the drug effects directly comparable. The three measurements were made on that single cell.

A direction preference that remains after one drug shows that the blocked pathway is not essential by itself. Other inputs or inherited tuning can keep the preference in place. Gabazine and strychnine were applied separately to the same neuron. The result describes one pathway at a time. A single neuron can depend on one inhibitory input and not the other.

A receptor class by itself is not enough to fix that outcome. Each neuron's arrangement of inputs sets its own outcome. Two neurons with the same receptor class can respond differently to the same sweep. Each drug condition used the same sweeps, and the outcome was read from those responses. This covers each neuron's inputs.

inserts.title: A 3.5-ms shift flips the preference
paragraphs: Negative and positive arrival values in the two-tone test give the relative order of two inputs. In the published example, the inhibitory input shifted by 3.5 ms in that order. Before the shift, inhibition arrived first. Those values came from the two-tone measurements of the same neuron. The arrival values were measured in milliseconds. Those values were negative before the shift.

Measurable suppression still existed after the shift. The timing of that suppression had changed, though its size had not. Late inhibition could not stop an early excitatory response. The neuron responded to upward sweeps that earlier inhibition had blocked. The neuron had responded strongly to downward sweeps before the drug. Its response to upward sweeps was small before blockade.

Selectivity in this example depended on the order of inputs more than on their size. Changing when the suppression arrives changed the preference. Its strength was measurable at the end of the shift. The shift changed the timing of one input alone. Timing alone changed the preference in that example. The example puts the order of inputs in focus.

inserts.title: Glycine and sideband suppression agree
paragraphs: The pharmacological result agrees with the earlier spectral-removal test. Two manipulations gave matching results on rate tuning. Removing high frequencies from the stimulus and blocking glycine receptors both produced a similar change. Each manipulation tested the same sideband from a different side. Both manipulations changed rate tuning in the same direction. Both results agree on the sideband.

The other manipulation removes a local receptor role in the suppression. Together, the two results implicate the same sideband. Each test isolated a different step of the suppression. Agreement between separate methods strengthens the case for a sideband effect. Glycine receptors mediate the inhibitory input at that site. The two methods are separate, so their agreement carries weight.

The gabazine examples kept their high-frequency suppression and fast-pass preference. Gabazine left this sideband intact. In the strychnine example, the sideband was eliminated, so the rate tuning changed with it. The same pattern held for the rate tuning, which fell with the sideband. Rate tuning stayed intact in those gabazine neurons. The contrast between the two drugs is the central result.

A decline in the combined measure may not come from failed detection alone. An attempt can fail after detection has occurred. Some approaches end in a miss or an abort instead of a capture. Each of those outcomes is counted in a separate category. Attempts and captures respond to clutter in different ways. Clutter affects each step in the sequence.

The open-room condition gave the baseline for these categories. Near the vegetation, echoes from the plant arrived alongside the echo from the insect. 2: Big brown bats emit **FM sweeps**, calls whose frequency falls during each call. Each call has two strong harmonics. The first harmonic, FM1, sweeps from about 55 to 25 kHz. The second harmonic, FM2, sweeps from about 110 to 50 kHz. The two harmonics are related by a twofold frequency ratio. Both fall within one broadcast.

These wide sweeps differ from a constant-frequency call, which holds one frequency. Each part of the sweep is sent at a different moment. Changes in frequency over time carry timing information. An echo preserves the timing of each frequency, so the bat receives the order in which the sound was sent and returned.

Behavioral filtering experiments test the two harmonics separately. Bats can judge echo delay with FM1 alone. When FM1 frequencies are missing, FM2 offers no substitute. Filtering removes one harmonic while the rest of the call stays in place. The result shows that FM1 carries information that FM2 lacks. The test isolates what each harmonic provides.
3: **Echo delay** is the time between an outgoing call and its returning echo. Sound travels from the bat to the target and back again. A more distant target sends back a later echo, because its sound covers more distance. **Target range** is the distance from the bat to the target. Longer delays mean farther targets.

Simmons trained bats to discriminate target distance. Electronic delay channels could change the arrival time of each echo. The loudspeakers stayed at fixed physical positions throughout. The timing changed, while the location of each loudspeaker stayed put. This arrangement left the physical setup unchanged across all conditions. The timing alone then carried the cue.

This separation allowed a direct test of the ranging cue. The bat judged relative simulated distance from echo arrival time alone. The loudspeaker's real distance never changed. Arrival time carried the whole judgment. The result isolates the timing cue from every physical location cue. The judgment depended on timing, not on where the loudspeaker sat.
4: Simmons trained bats to choose the nearer of two targets. Each correct choice led to food at the landing platform beside the nearer target. The bat had to compare the two echoes before it moved. Each decision had a clear answer, so the reward tracked accuracy. The task asked which target lay closer to the bat.

One target stayed at a fixed range, such as 30 or 60 cm. The other was brought progressively closer to it. The bat was tested on whether it could still pick the nearer target as the gap narrowed. Each step of the gap produced a new choice. The series ran until the two targets were equally far away.

Accuracy fell as the distance difference approached zero. When both targets sat at equal distances, the bats reached chance. The procedure measured how finely bats resolve differences in range between two targets. The bats never judged one target alone, so absolute distance was outside the task. Each comparison involved two targets presented together.

Synchronized ultrasound recordings and high-speed video were combined into reconstructed three-dimensional flight paths. An open-room condition served as the control without the plant's echoes. Each trial recorded the sounds and the flight together. The bats were free to fly during the trials.

With the insect 10 cm from vegetation, bats hit or captured it in about 40 percent of trials. They made no attempt in nearly half. Hits or captures rose to almost 80 percent at 20 cm and about 90 percent at 40 cm. Open-room performance was nearly complete. Each condition varied the spacing between insect and plant.

Clutter reduced both the willingness to attempt an interception and the success once the bat approached. The combined hit-or-capture measure is broader than successful consumption. The difficulty appears at these particular vegetation spacings. The spacing sets how hard each capture is. The vegetation made successful capture less likely at close spacing. The categories show the stage of failure.
43: Bats in the Moss experiment often flew alongside the vegetation and the insect before turning toward the target. The approach was not a straight line through the plant's strongest echo direction. The flight geometry changed the angle between prey and background. The route itself carried the bat around the clutter. The bats adjusted their path before turning.

As the insect moved closer to the vegetation, the final direct approach grew shorter and the late turn grew sharper. Three-dimensional trajectories and emitted pulse intervals were measured together. The strongest changes in turning happened in the final 50 to 100 ms before contact. Those late changes were the largest. Each change followed the insect's distance.

The authors read these trajectories as reducing interference. By flying this way, the bat ensonified the prey off axis from the vegetation for part of the approach. This interpretation rests on the geometry, not on a recording of the bat's internal spatial map. The map was never measured. The bats' behavior was the measured quantity.
44: **Sonar strobe groups** are clusters of calls separated from neighboring calls or groups by longer intervals. Moss and colleagues identified groups with stable internal intervals when they contained three or more sounds. Grouping occurred during the approach, before the terminal capture phase. The groups appeared as the bat neared its prey. Stable internal intervals defined each group.

Within each group, pulse intervals shortened as the bat closed in on its target. Calls in the clutter conditions tended to fall into groups with shorter intervals than calls in the open room. The grouping added structure beyond a general rise in call rate. The groups had a pattern of their own.

The authors proposed that repeated sampling at stable intervals could sharpen the spatial representation of the scene. The study measured vocal timing and behavior. It recorded vocal timing and behavior, and the perceptual benefit remains a hypothesis. The benefit is a proposal, not a measurement. The perceptual part of the claim is still open.
45: The **terminal buzz** is the rapid-call sequence right before prey interception. Moss and colleagues defined buzz-II calls by pulse intervals of 10 ms or less. They compared buzz duration across plant-target separations and the open-room condition. The buzz was measured at every separation. Shorter buzz durations were the main outcome of that comparison.

Mean buzz-II duration fell from more than 300 ms in the open room to about 200 ms at 40 cm from vegetation and about 100 ms at 10 cm. Prey capture still succeeded sometimes with the shorter buzz, including at the closest separation. The shorter buzz still led to captures. The buzz shortened at every separation tested.

The authors proposed that extended clutter echoes make prolonged rapid calling less useful. The observed shortening ties vocal timing to scene structure. Successful interception combined changes in call groups, final approach geometry and buzz duration. The buzz was one of several changes. The shortened buzz changes the timing of the final approach. Each measure is part of one interception.
